mcqs.question: Why is the slow-write/fast-read array compaction pattern O(1) extra space?
options: Because the write pointer never advances past the read pointer, so it only ever overwrites cells that have already been fully read
Because it uses recursion instead of loops
Because arrays are always passed by reference in every language
Because it only works correctly on arrays below a fixed size threshold
mcqs.explanation: write always trails or ties read, so any cell it overwrites has already been consumed by read on an earlier or the same step — nothing needed later is lost, and no second array is allocated. Pass-by-reference semantics and recursion have nothing to do with the space bound.

mcqs.question: In Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array, why compare against arr[write - 1] rather than arr[read - 1]?
options: arr[read - 1] is undefined when read equals 0
arr[write - 1] is the last value actually kept, which can differ from the last value scanned once duplicates have been skipped
Using arr[read - 1] would always throw an index-out-of-bounds error
There's no functional difference; both comparisons are equivalent
mcqs.explanation: Once even one duplicate has been skipped, read and write diverge, so the last value seen (arr[read-1]) is not necessarily the last value kept (arr[write-1]) — comparing against the wrong one would let a duplicate slip through. The loop starts at read=1, so read-1 is always valid; it's simply the wrong reference point.

mcqs.question: In Move Zeroes, why does swapping arr[write] and arr[read] work where a plain overwrite would fail?
options: Swapping is required to avoid a runtime type error in most languages
Overwriting is asymptotically slower than swapping
Swapping avoids needing any comparison logic at all
A plain overwrite would discard the zero already sitting at write, while swapping relocates it to where read currently is, keeping it in the array
mcqs.explanation: Once write < read, arr[write] holds a zero that a plain overwrite would silently erase; swapping instead moves that zero forward to read's position, which is exactly where a zero belongs relative to the elements not yet scanned. Both approaches are O(n), and neither avoids the need to compare against zero.

mcqs.question: Why can Find the Duplicate Number be solved with Floyd's tortoise-and-hare instead of a hash set?
options: Because sorting the array first makes the duplicate trivially identifiable without any extra algorithm
Interpreting arr[i] as a pointer to index arr[i] turns the repeated value into a cycle, which is exactly the structure Floyd's algorithm detects
Because tortoise-and-hare is asymptotically faster than a hash set in every case
Because the array is guaranteed to already contain negative values marking the cycle
mcqs.explanation: Reinterpreting each value as an index turns the array into a function from indices to indices; a repeated value forces two indices to map to the same target, which is precisely what creates a cycle that Floyd's algorithm can find in O(1) space. Sorting and hash sets both work too but cost O(n log n) time or O(n) space respectively — that's the actual reason to prefer this trick, not raw speed.

mcqs.question: Why does the array-as-cycle duplicate-finding trick require every value to be in range [1, n]?
options: So the array can be sorted quickly using counting sort as a fallback
Every value must double as a valid array index for the 'next' step, which is what makes the walk well-defined and provably cyclic
Values must be positive to avoid negative indices, though the specific upper bound n doesn't actually matter
It doesn't matter; the trick applies to any array of integers regardless of range
mcqs.explanation: The whole proof depends on treating a value as the next index to visit — if a value fell outside [1, n], it either wouldn't index into the array or would collide with an unrelated slot, breaking the one-to-one indices-map-to-indices structure the cycle argument relies on. The upper bound matters exactly as much as the lower one.
